articles.headlineTranslated: Measles infection in a man in his 40s from Fukui Prefecture; traveled to Vietnam in late April, returned home by car from Kanagawa.
articles.summary: As of May 12, 2026, Fukui Prefecture reported a measles infection in a man in his 40s, who recovered at home. He had traveled to Vietnam in late April, with infection thought most probable there. Fever began May 6; he sought care May 8; rash appeared May 10; measles virus was confirmed May 11. He returned to Fukui by private car from Kanagawa on May 6 and has since avoided public transport. Authorities advised suspected cases to contact medical facilities before visiting and to avoid public transit. Measles virus can survive in air for under two hours; typical progression includes fever and cold-like symptoms about 10 days after exposure, followed by high fever and a widespread rash with Koplik spots in the mouth. Nationally, 436 measles cases had been reported as of April 26.

articles.headlineTranslated: Measles outbreak you can't ignore: First call the hospital before seeking medical care — Asahi Shimbun
articles.summary: Measles outbreak in Japan accelerates, with 299 lab-confirmed cases as of April 15, 2026, surpassing the 2019 high of 744. Although the WHO still recognizes Japan as an elimination country, the virus is believed to be imported from overseas, with clusters including schools and transmission reported across Asia, Africa, the Middle East, Europe, and the Americas. Data from the National Institute for Public Health Crisis Management show over 80% of patients are aged 15–49, led by 20–39-year-olds. Japan’s two-dose measles vaccination program became routine in 2006; many older cohorts received only one dose, leaving immunity gaps. In FY2024, coverage for the two-dose schedule at 1 year and at pre-elementary school entry was 92% and 91%, below the 95% target. Measles is highly airborne and not readily prevented by handwashing or masks; vaccination remains the sole effective preventive measure. The author recalls a 2019 incident when a red rash appeared during a meeting, prompting immediate contact with a hospital.

articles.headlineTranslated: COVID-19: Three years under Category 5—Keep up preventive measures
articles.summary: COVID-19 in Japan remains under Category 5 for three years (since May 2023), with ongoing preventive measures emphasized for the elderly and those with underlying conditions. National sentinel data show shrinking waves: summer peaks per medical institution fell from about 20 patients in 2023 to about 8 in 2025, and winter peaks from roughly 16 (2023–24) to under 3 this year. Healthy young adults mostly experience mild illness and may not seek care, but hospitalizations and deaths remain heavily concentrated among those aged 65+, with frailty and cognitive decline post-infection. Elderly-care facilities reinforce routine temperature checks, hand hygiene, and masking. While overall suppression continues, avoiding clusters is essential. Since initial domestic detection in 2020, policy shifted to standard medical funding; elderly vaccination subsidies ended and uptake declined. The circulating virus is Omicron-related, with a shifting sublineage. Measles cases are rising in Japan; seek medical advice if infection is suspected.

articles.headlineTranslated: What Edo-era Measles Pictures Teach About the Transmission of Disease: COVID-19 Lessons That Linger Even in Useless Things
articles.summary: Measles is spreading in Japan as of 2026-05-10. Measles is a highly airborne infectious disease that can be severe even in the same room, and the Edo-era population feared it greatly due to the absence of a vaccine. The 1862 Edo outbreak (Bunka 2) reportedly caused over 14,000 deaths in Edo. At that time, ukiyo-e artists produced ‘measles pictures’ depicting the illness. The article uses these historical images to illustrate transmission and draws COVID-19–related lessons that linger in cultural artifacts, suggesting that artifacts can illuminate how diseases spread beyond direct medical contexts. It contrasts historical fear with modern outbreaks and emphasizes airborne transmission and the ongoing relevance of public health measures.

articles.headlineTranslated: Osamu Suzuki shocked by the measles vaccine's "gap generation": "Did I not get vaccinated?"
articles.summary: Measles outbreak in Japan intensifies, with infections through April 2026 about 4.5 times higher than the same period last year, partly attributed to increased inbound tourism. Vaccination schemes vary by birth cohort: two-dose schedules for those born on or after April 2, 2000; one-dose for those born between October 1, 1972 and April 1, 2000; and likely no routine vaccination for those born before October 1, 1972, creating a so-called 'gap-generation' of under-immunized individuals. Osamu Suzuki, 54, expresses shock at potentially belonging to the older cohort. A 1995-born announcer reported two doses but serology showed insufficient antibody titers, indicating a possible need for a booster. Public health advice emphasizes checking maternal-child health records, pursuing antibody testing if unsure, and noting that some local authorities subsidize testing. The discussion underscores vaccination gaps and immunity verification amid ongoing measles spread in Japan."

articles.summary: Measles in Japan: On Apr 20–26, 2026, 68 new measles cases were reported nationwide, bringing the January-to-date total to 436 and signaling a pace near the 2019 peak (744 for the year-to-date period). The year’s weekly total (68) is the highest so far. Age group 10–30 accounts for about 74% of cases. Tokyo hosts 211 cases, nearly half of the national total; Saitama, Chiba, and Kanagawa together reach 304; Kagoshima reports 34 during a cluster. Measles virus is highly transmissible via airborne exposure in shared spaces. Symptoms emerge after roughly 10 days and include fever, cough, runny nose, and rash; encephalitis is a severe risk. Despite WHO declaring Japan measles-eliminated in 2015, importations from travelers sustain transmission. Vaccination with the measles-rubella (MR) vaccine—two doses at ages 1 and before elementary school—remains essential.

Tokyo accounts for 211 cases, Kanagawa 40, with Saitama and Chiba also contributing; four prefectures total 304 cases, and Kagoshima reported 34 cases from a cluster. Measles is highly contagious and can spread by airborne transmission; symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose, and rash, with possible death in severe cases. Japan is in a measles elimination state for indigenous virus, but imported cases circulate via travelers; authorities say vaccination is critical. They urge routine childhood immunization, and recommend vaccination for people in contact with children, tourism workers, and airport staff who are unvaccinated.

articles.summary: Hantavirus infection on a cruise ship after Golden Week, with fatalities, prompted comparisons to the Diamond Princess COVID-19 outbreak in 2020. About 150 people aboard, including Japanese, are affected. No vaccine or antiviral exists; transmission is linked to contact with infected rodents rather than sustained human-to-human spread, so containment hinges on identifying the rodent reservoir and blocking routes of exposure. The article emphasizes three basic outbreak elements and notes that, unlike COVID-19 or measles, hantavirus manages spread primarily through contact with the animal source, not prolonged close contact between people. Precautions for travelers include avoiding rodent encounters in endemic areas. Domestic spread in Japan is regarded as unlikely, and imported/exported risk is considered low by authorities. European risk is described as very low by ECDC in related assessments. The article cites May 6, 2026, information from Japan’s National Crisis Management and public health sources.

articles.headlineTranslated: Measles infection is spreading even among the two-dose vaccinated generation! What should be done for measles countermeasures?
articles.summary: Measles outbreaks in Japan in 2026 total 299 infections as of April 15, with 56 new cases in the past week. Tokyo accounts for 108 cases (36% of the national total), and 35 new cases in the week. In Shinjuku, a primary school outbreak caused class closures; 18 infections among students and staff since April 9, indicating local transmission. Immunity: one measles dose provides about 93–95% protection; two-dose MR vaccination yields high seropositivity. Since 2006, Japan has used a two-dose schedule (first dose at 1 year, booster before elementary school). Yet outbreaks have occurred among two-dose individuals, showing vaccines reduce severity and transmission but don’t fully prevent infection in crowded settings. Younger cohorts show waning antibody levels; 71% of cases are aged 15–39. 2024 MR vaccination rate fell to 91% from ~95%. The article urges catch-up vaccination for incomplete immunizations and verification of MR vaccination; vaccines cost about 10,000 yen per dose.

Public warnings note possible importations from overseas amid ongoing outbreaks; Haneda Airport displayed alerts on April 30. articles.summary: Measles cases in Tokyo reached 153 as of April 19, the highest in Japan, about fivefold the previous year. A measles outbreak prompted grade-level closures at an elementary school in Shinjuku Ward for the first time in 12 years, with 47 confirmed infections (41 students, 6 staff). Vaccination status remains unclear: 7 patients were unvaccinated or had only one dose, 28 had two doses yet were infected, and 12 cases are under investigation. The National Institute for Health Crisis Management Research reports roughly seven in ten current patients have one or no doses, or have unknown vaccination histories. Tokyo Governor Yuriko Koike urged verification of vaccination history via the maternal and child health handbook, and advised those with unverified records to seek antibody testing or vaccination consultation at medical facilities. Two-dose vaccination is protective, but status remains uncertain for many.

articles.summary: Measles is spreading globally, with rising infections in Japan. Patients present with fever above 39°C and widespread rash; mortality can reach about 1 in 1,000. In Sapporo, Dr. Jun Tamai warns Japan’s domestic increase mirrors global outbreaks, especially in Southeast Asia, the United Kingdom, and Canada. The WHO had eliminated measles in Canada (2025) and the UK (2026) as countries achieving measles elimination, but that status has since been withdrawn. The post-COVID surge in international travel is viewed as a contributing factor. Prevention centers on vaccination: Japan’s routine two-dose schedule (one dose at 1 year and a second before elementary school) and national aim for 95% coverage for herd immunity. However current coverage is below 95%, and vaccination rates have declined since the pandemic. Clinicians are advised to evaluate travelers returning from outbreak countries as potentially infected.

articles.summary: Measles vaccination before travel to Japan is debated as Tokyo and surrounding prefectures report a measles outbreak. A former infectious disease physician and travel expert said travelers should not assume they need extra MMR doses for trips to Japan; current cases are concentrated in Tokyo and nearby prefectures, with sporadic transmission elsewhere. Measles remains circulating globally, including in the United States, with risk levels hard to quantify. Individuals should assess their status: verify age-appropriate vaccination, existing immunity, and antibodies. MMR is highly effective; two childhood doses, plus any recent boosters, may sustain antibodies for roughly 15 years or more. Taiwan reported its first domestic measles case imported from Japan since 2019, and Taiwan's CDC raised travel alert to Attention. Adults born after 1966 may have waning immunity; consult a hospital 2–4 weeks before travel. During stay, wash hands, avoid touching the face, and wear a mask.

articles.summary: Measles outbreaks in Japan are expanding at the fastest pace since 2020, crossing age groups as many adults in their 30s–50s have only one vaccine dose. The virus is highly contagious by air, making large holiday travel high risk. As of April 22, 2026, Japan recorded 362 measles patients, with about 70% in the Tokyo metropolitan area (1 prefecture plus six others). In Kita Ward, Tokyo, a 41-year-old man caring for an infant sought MMR vaccination after antibody testing showed insufficient immunity. Vaccine supply is generally stable, but local shortages occur due to rising demand; officials urge securing two-dose coverage, prioritizing school-entry doses. Generational differences: those born 1972–1990 are typically one-dose; 1990–2000 may have two doses; born after 2000 standard is two doses. Symptoms include fever, rash, conjunctivitis; complications include encephalitis and pneumonia; fatality about 0.1%. Prevention hinges on vaccination and cautious behavior during outbreaks.

articles.summary: Measles infections are rapidly expanding in Japan, with 362 cases reported as of April 19, 2026—the second fastest pace in a decade. In the Chubu region's nine prefectures, Aichi prefecture experienced a cluster, while Tokyo leads nationwide and Kagoshima also reports a cluster. The measles virus is highly infectious, estimated to spread to 12–18 people from a single case in susceptible groups; household transmission can reach ~90%. Incubation is 10–12 days, followed by high fever and rash; pneumonia or encephalitis can occur, with infants and pregnant women at higher risk. About 70% of cases are aged 10–30s. Two-dose vaccination is protective; 2024–2025 coverage was 91% vs a 95% target. Many adults in their 30s–50s have only one dose; MR vaccination is available at roughly 10,000–15,000 yen. Post-exposure vaccination within 72 hours can prevent disease; during holidays avoid public transport if symptomatic and ensure pre-travel vaccination for outbreak areas.

articles.summary: Measles cases in Japan are expanding, with 299 infections confirmed as of January 15 and this trend on pace to exceed the 2019 peak of 744. Although Japan is recognized by WHO as an elimination country, infections are imported and school clusters have occurred; outbreaks are reported across Asia, Africa, the Middle East, Europe, and the Americas. Data from the National Institute of Health Crisis Management show over 80% of patients are aged 15–49, with 20–39 making up about half. Japan’s two-dose measles vaccination began in 2006, previously one dose, yet many people still had only one dose, leaving immunity gaps. Two-dose targets by age 1 and before elementary school are 95%+, but 2024 rates were 92% and 91%. Measles is airborne; vaccination is essential, not handwashing or masks. Hospitals face strain; patients are urged to call ahead before seeking care. The author recalls a May 2019 anecdote illustrating vigilance.
